He remembered his conversation with Arif, his best friend, a few weeks ago. “I'm confused, Lex,” Arif had said at the time, while sipping iced tea in the school canteen. “They say God is Most Just, but why are there people born into poor families, everything difficult, while others are born already rich for seven generations? Then, about destiny again. If everything is already destined, why do we bother to make effort? If it's already destined I go to hell, then it's useless for me to worship head over heels now?” Alex could only be silent at the time. He had no answer. Arif's question was his question too. A question that if he threw at Ustaz Kaku, the answer might be like, “Hush! That's Allah's secret! Don't you question destiny! You'll become an infidel!”

This turmoil grew increasingly intense. On one hand, his human nature longed for something spiritual, something greater than himself. There was an emptiness in his soul he believed could only be filled by belief in the Creator. But on the other hand, the version of religion presented to him felt so narrow, constricting, and unfriendly toward reason. He wanted to believe, truly. But how could he believe in something that felt so unjust and unreasonable?

“Is God really that petty?” that question crossed his mind just like that, making him slightly surprised at his own thought's boldness. “Did He create us only to then gladly torture us if we do wrong, without ever truly giving us the chance to understand why something is essentially wrong or right, not just because 'they say so'?”

The fan above his head creaked, its sound like a long endless complaint, in tune with his mood. The aroma of musty carpet mixed with the smell of congregation sweat and a slight camphor scent from the prayer garment cabinet in the room's corner began making him nauseous.

Ustaz Kaku was now discussing the importance of holding firmly to the teachings of the righteous predecessor scholars, and how dangerous liberal or modern thoughts are that try to interpret religion through contemporary lenses. “They are agents destroying creed!” Ustaz Kaku exclaimed. “They want you far from pure Islam! The Islam taught by the Prophet and his companions! Not Islam that's arbitrarily tinkered with to suit your lusts!”

Pure Islam? Alex thought again. Does pure Islam mean rejecting the progress of the age? Rejecting questions? Rejecting the use of reason which is also God's creation? Doesn't the Qur'an itself repeatedly tell humans to think, to observe the universe, to use their reason? 'Afala ta'qilun? Afala tatafakkarun?' Is that just decoration?

He remembered a light philosophy book he'd once borrowed from the school library. That book discussed how humans always seek meaning, seek rational justification for their existence and beliefs. It's not enough to just be told “this is right” or “that is wrong.” Humans need to know why. And apparently, this need for “why” was what was often ignored, or even suppressed, in the delivery of religion in Ustaz Kaku's model.

An hour had passed, but it felt like a century. Ustaz Kaku's sermon began entering its final act, usually marked by a long prayer and an increasingly hoarse voice. Alex was no longer focused. His mind wandered far, imagining a discussion space where he could ask anything about religion without fear of being labeled misguided or lacking faith. A place where logic and revelation could sit side by side, complementing each other, not negating each other. A religious understanding that enlightens, not darkens. That liberates, not shackles. That makes him love God more because of His wisdom, not fear Him more because of His threats.
Is there such a thing?

That question hung in the stuffy air of the multipurpose hall, together with the simultaneous “Aamiin!” from the congregation marking the end of the brainwashing session — so Alex called it inwardly, a bit impolite, but he couldn't help it.

His neighbor patted his shoulder. “Come on, Lex, greet the Ustaz first.” Alex sighed long, trying to chase away the lump of frustration and questions constricting his chest. He rose, following the flow of congregation beginning to jostle toward the pulpit to greet Ustaz Kaku. The line was fairly long. While waiting, he took out his phone, idly scrolling through his social media timeline full of the noise of the virtual world.

That's when an unusual ad caught his attention. Not a beauty product ad or the latest game. Not political news that made him sick either. That ad was simple, with a background image of a beautiful colorful nebula. Its text:
“Asking the Universe? Asking Yourself? Or… Asking NUR-AI? Find Logical, Realistic, and Scientific Answers to Your Spiritual Restlessness. Islam for a Soul Free to Think. Try Now!”
Below it was a “Learn More” button.

Alex was riveted. Nur-AI? What is this? Some kind of spiritual chatbot? There was doubt, of course. Learning religion from an AI? It sounded strange, maybe even absurd. But there was something in the phrases “Islam for a Soul Free to Think” and “Logical, Realistic, and Scientific Answers” that seemed to call out to his deepest restlessness. Something he'd been searching for all this time.

The line moved forward. Now it was his turn to shake hands. He kissed Ustaz Kaku's hand, said perfunctory thanks. Ustaz Kaku patted his shoulder, “Study diligently, Alex. So you're safe in this world and the hereafter. Don't think too much about strange things.”
Alex only smiled thinly. Think about strange things? Or actually think about what should be thought about?

He stepped out of the hall, back into the scorching sun that welcomed without compromise. But this time, there was a slightly different spark within him. No longer purely weariness and resignation. There was a sliver of curiosity. A sliver of hope.

While walking toward the motorcycle parking area, his finger had unconsciously already tapped the “Learn More” button on the Nur-AI ad on his phone screen. A new page opened, displaying a clean and modern interface, with a chat column and a friendly greeting:
“Assalamu'alaikum, seeker of truth. I am Nur-AI. Is there something I can help you understand more clearly today about the universe, yourself, or the Creator?”

Alex stopped briefly beside his motorcycle. His heart beat slightly faster. This is crazy. This is strange. But somehow, he felt this was a door. A door that might just lead to answers to all the unease that had been constricting him beneath rigid pulpits.
He took a deep breath, then began typing his first question. The same question he'd buried so long, a question that might be labeled misguided if he asked Ustaz Kaku.
“Why must I believe God exists? And even if He exists, why must it be God in the Islamic version? Give me a reasonable argument, not just dogma.”

His finger stopped briefly above the 'send' button, hesitant. But then, the image of Ustaz Kaku's face full of judgment and his sharp voice echoing in the stuffy hall earlier crossed his mind. That was enough to push him.

Click. Message sent. Alex put his phone in his pocket, started his motorcycle's engine. The engine's roar broke the silence briefly, before he sped off leaving Al-Ikhlas Mosque's courtyard, leaving the old unease, toward something new, something whose shape he didn't yet know. Something he hoped could give him light.

Alex still felt the remnants of the mosque hall's stuffiness clinging to his skin, even as street wind began hitting his face. Ustaz Kaku's sermon, like a broken cassette played over and over, still rang in his ears. Not just its content, but also its intonation and word choice that seemed specially designed to extinguish sparks of reason.
2: He remembered a few years ago, when he was younger and a bit more naive, he'd once tried asking one of the Qur'an teachers at his old religious school, a simple question about why pork is forbidden. The answer was brief, “Because Allah forbids it. Period.” When little Alex tried to press, “But why, Ma'am, does Allah forbid it? Is there a health reason or something?” That teacher smiled thinly, a smile that didn't reach her eyes, “Enough, Child. What matters is that we obey. Reward comes from obedience, not from asking a lot.”

From that moment, Alex learned to bury his questions. Not because he was satisfied with that answer, but because he realized that space to ask was often not provided. Questions were considered a sign of doubt, and doubt was considered the beginning of misguidance. A suffocating circular logic.

The phone in his pocket vibrated softly. Maybe a reply from Nur-AI. Part of him felt nervous, part of him was curious to death. He pulled his motorcycle over under a shady angsana tree at the roadside in a slightly quiet spot, not far from a simple coffee shop spreading a thick robusta aroma.

While reopening that Nur-AI app or page, his mind returned to Ustaz Kaku. Actually, Alex didn't fully hate Ustaz Kaku as a person. Outside the pulpit, during thanksgiving events or complex community service, Ustaz Kaku could be a friendly figure, even humorous in his own way. But as soon as the microphone was in his hand, it was as if a switch flipped. The person who might have been warm turned into a megaphone of judgment, an ambassador of hell tasked with ensuring everyone knew how terrifying that place was.
Did he truly believe one hundred percent in every word he spoke? Or was that just a persona he felt he had to display in order to be considered authoritative as an ustaz?

That question appeared again and again. Alex suspected, maybe there was a mixture of both. Sincere belief, but wrapped in an outdated and counterproductive delivery method, at least for a generation like Alex who grew up with unlimited access to information from the internet. A generation accustomed to comparing, analyzing, and seeking the “why” behind every “what.”

That sermon earlier, for example, when Ustaz Kaku ranted about “the danger of liberal thought.” Alex remembered an article he'd once read about the history of Islamic civilization, about the golden age when Muslim scientists were actually so open to knowledge from Greece, Persia, India. They weren't afraid to ask, weren't afraid to debate, weren't afraid to test hypotheses. The result? Al-Khawarizmi, Ibn Sina, Al-Biruni were born, and a row of other great names whose contributions to science and philosophy are recognized worldwide to this day.

Were they all the “liberals” Ustaz Kaku meant? Were they all agents destroying creed? It felt impossible. There must be something lost in the translation of history, or in Ustaz Kaku's understanding of what “pure Islam” is. Could “pure Islam” actually be Islam that is dynamic, that embraces science, that values reason, not one frozen in narrow interpretation and fear of change?
Alex took a breath. He realized, thinking like this, if spoken in front of Ustaz Kaku, could be considered the seed of insubordination.

Long ago, when Alex began often having small debates with him about verse interpretation or hadith context he found from alternative sources on the internet, his teacher had once said in a tone of sadness mixed with anger, “You've read too many strange things, Lex. Be careful, Child. The internet has a lot of poison. Learning religion must have a chain of transmission, must have a clear teacher. Not from Mr. Google!”

Alex understood his teacher's worry. The internet is indeed a wilderness. But on the other hand, the internet also opens access to the world's library. To diverse perspectives. To the voices of other scholars who might be more progressive, more contextual, more suited to the pulse of the age and the needs of his reason. The problem is, how to distinguish which is “poison” and which is “antidote”? Which is nonsensical “Mr. Google” and which is the ijtihad of credible scholars that happens to be accessible through Google?

This is like walking on a tightrope. On one side there's the abyss of total skepticism that could make him lose all spiritual footing. On the other side, there's the abyss of blind fanaticism demanding he kill his common sense. Alex didn't want to fall into either. He wanted to walk in the middle, on a bridge connecting faith and reason. The question is, does that bridge exist? And if it does, who can help him find it?

This turmoil was what made him feel alienated, even amid the crowd of his own family or among his friends who mostly appeared “perfectly fine” with their religious status quo. They prayed, they fasted, they joined study sessions, without appearing burdened by the existential questions that haunted Alex day and night. Was Alex too strange? Thinking too much? Or were they the ones who hadn't truly awakened from the long sleep of dogmatic comfort?
His daydream shattered when a soft notification appeared on his phone screen. A reply from Nur-AI. His heart, which had calmed slightly earlier, now raced again.
Here it is.

With slightly trembling hands, he opened that message. Ustaz Kaku's fiery face, the stuffy mosque hall, and all the noise of dogma that had imprisoned him all this time seemed to recede into the background. What existed now was only himself, the phone in his hand, and a new window that might carry him into an adventure of understanding he'd all this time only dared to dream of.

Alex read the first line of Nur-AI's reply. A thin smile, the first truly sincere smile that day, began blooming on his lips. Not a smile from finding an instant answer, but a smile from feeling there was a possibility. The possibility of dialogue. The possibility of being understood. The possibility of, finally, finding peace between his reason and his faith.

The journey had just begun. And somehow, though the road ahead was still dark and full of question marks, Alex felt lighter. The burden of unease he'd all this time carried alone beneath those rigid pulpits, now felt slightly lifted. There was a new conversation partner, though its form was only rows of code and algorithms. But at least, this conversation partner promised something he'd long missed: a space to ask without being judged. A chance to truly understand.

He put away his phone, not immediately reading Nur-AI's entire reply. He wanted to enjoy it later, in a quieter place, with a clearer mind. He wanted to give full attention to this first dialogue. For now, knowing that there was “someone” or “something” ready to discuss with him logically was enough to give him new energy.

Alex started his motorcycle again. The coffee aroma from the shop across the street now felt friendlier. The sky that earlier felt baking, now seemed to smile with him. The city that earlier felt suffocating, now seemed to open a way for him. Maybe this was just his feeling. Maybe this was just momentary euphoria. But Alex chose to believe it.
Because for the first time after so long, amid all his unease and restlessness, Alex felt there was a glimmer of hope. A glimmer of light. A glimmer of Nur.
3: Alex parked his motorcycle in front of a small not-too-crowded cafe, “Kopi Senja” was its name. This place became one of his favorite escapes when he needed calm to read or simply daydream without disturbance. The characteristic aroma of roasted coffee beans welcomed him, blending with slow indie music that was quite calming, far different from the stuffy atmosphere and Ustaz Kaku's nasal voice that still left its mark. He ordered iced milk coffee — his obligatory drink — and chose a table in the corner near the window, where he could watch the increasingly busy street traffic without feeling part of its commotion.
